case_studies.title: Fighting Numerical Hallucinations via Data-centric Compilation for Online Financial QA
case_studies.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly advanced online data services, particularly in the domain of financial question answering (FinQA). However, such systems remain susceptible to numerical reasoning hallucinations, which critically undermine reliability in high-stakes financial applications. Although retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has been widely adopted to ground responses in external knowledge, it introduces three persistent challenges: noise sensitivity, calculation fragility, and an auditability crisis. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of numerical hallucinations in large language models used for financial question answering, by building a data-centric compilation approach, resulting in more reliable and accurate financial data services. The approach aims to reduce errors in financial calculations and provide more trustworthy responses. This research is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.

case_studies.title: SpecDB: LLM-Generated Customized Databases via Feature-Oriented Decomposition
case_studies.abstract: Mainstream relational databases ship a uniform feature set across deployments, although individual workloads exercise only a fraction of the available subsystems. We investigate whether a database can instead be generated on demand with a feature set matched to the target workload. We present SpecDB, a system that uses large language models (LLMs) to synthesize customized relational databases. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of one-size-fits-all databases by building a system called SpecDB, which uses large language models to generate customized relational databases for specific workloads. The result is a more efficient database that only includes the features needed for the target workload. This innovation could lead to more optimized database performance and reduced resource usage.

This makes the reliability of open-weight models a deployment issue. case_studies.title: UniAudio-Token: Empowering Semantic Speech Tokenizers with General Audio Perception
case_studies.abstract: Semantic speech tokenizers have become a widely used interface for Audio-LLMs, owing to their compact single-codebook design and strong linguistic alignment. However, their focus on linguistic abstraction induces acoustic blindness, limiting their applicability beyond speech-centric tasks. We propose UniAudio-Token, a framework that empowers semantic tokenizers with general audio perception without compromising speech ability. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of acoustic blindness in semantic speech tokenizers by introducing a framework called UniAudio-Token, which empowers tokenizers with general audio perception without compromising speech ability. The researchers built a framework that mitigates information loss through Semantic-Acoustic Primitives and Multi-Granularity Encoding. The result is a more versatile tokenizer that can handle tasks beyond speech-centric ones.

case_studies.title: Preference-Aware Rubric Learning for Personalized Evaluation
case_studies.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) evolve from general-purpose assistants to user-centric agents, personalization has become central to aligning model behavior with individual preferences, making the evaluation of personalized alignment a critical bottleneck. Existing evaluation methods-ranging from automatic metrics to LLM-as-a-judge approaches-fail to capture subjective, user-specific preferences embedded in long-term interaction histories. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of evaluating personalized alignment in Large Language Models by building a preference-aware rubric learning system, which resulted in a more effective way to capture subjective user preferences. case_studies.title: If LLMs Have Human-Like Attributes, Then So Does Age of Empires II
case_studies.abstract: Much research has been carried out on large language models (LLMs) and LLM-powered agentic workflows. case_studies.title: LinTree: Improving LLM Reasoning with Explicitly Structured Search Histories
case_studies.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often solve reasoning problems by generating intermediate traces that explore and revise partial solutions. From a search perspective, these traces can be viewed as linearized search trees, where the model extends a partial solution, abandons it when it fails, and backtracks to try alternatives. Compared with traditional heuristic-guided search, such a policy has a potential advantage: it conditions on the whole search trace rather than only on the current local state. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of inefficient search methods in large language models, building a system called LinTree that improves reasoning with explicitly structured search histories, resulting in better solution exploration. The system conditions on the whole search trace rather than only on the current local state. This is not directly relevant to managing cloud infrastructure.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on improving large language models' reasoning capabilities.

case_studies.title: COLLEAGUE.SKILL: Automated AI Skill Generation via Expert Knowledge Distillation
case_studies.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly expected not only to complete isolated tasks, but also to carry bounded representations of human expertise, judgment, and interaction style. Building such person-grounded agents remains difficult because actionable knowledge associated with a person or role is usually embedded in heterogeneous traces rather than written as clean instructions. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of capturing human expertise in AI systems by building an automated system called COLLEAGUE.SKILL, which generates AI skills via expert knowledge distillation, resulting in more person-grounded AI agents. The system aims to distill heterogeneous traces of human expertise into inspectable and correctable formats. This research is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.

case_studies.title: Can Generative AI help people navigate Radical Moral Disagreements? The CONSIDER prototype
case_studies.abstract: Radical Moral Disagreements (RMDs) are highly polarising topics that are increasingly censored in everyday life, with growing evidence suggesting that this polarisation carries measurable costs to public mental health. To address these challenges, some researchers have proposed Large Language Models (LLMs) as a means to support more democratic deliberation and better moral reasoning. Yet existing tools are poorly calibrated to help people navigate RMDs, because of their intense and divisive characteristics.
